common_name: Elmohr Bearded Iris (Historic 1945 Dykes Medal Mulberry-Red Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Elmohr Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Elmohr, hybridized by P.A. Loomis and registered in 1942 from 'William Mohr' crossed with a red seedling, produces immense, well-cupped standards and broad, heavily veined falls in a color between reddish mulberry and dahlia purple. Considered a sensation when first shown, it won the Award of Merit in 1944 and the American Dykes Medal in 1945. Its aril-influenced parentage gives it unusually large flower size and heavy texture for its era. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the old woody center.

common_name: Missouri Bearded Iris (Historic 1937 Dykes Medal Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Missouri Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Missouri, hybridized by J.H. Grinter and registered in 1933 from 'Blue Ribbon' crossed with 'Sensation', was hailed in its day as one of the finest clear, clean blues ever raised, with a smooth enamel-like finish that shows violet in strong sun and pure blue on overcast days. It earned the Award of Merit in 1935 and the American Dykes Medal in 1937, and demand for it in Midwestern nursery catalogs routinely outstripped supply. Divide every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor.

common_name: Rameses Bearded Iris (Historic 1932 Dykes Medal Pink-and-Apricot Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Rameses Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Rameses, hybridized by Hans P. Sass from 'King Tut' crossed with 'Baldwin' and registered in 1928, bears light russet-vinaceous standards with a yellow glow at the center over tourmaline-pink falls carrying a heavy apricot beard. A vigorous, fast-increasing, free-blooming plant that performs reliably across regions, it won the American Dykes Medal in 1932, one of the earliest winners of the award. Divide every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Mary Geddes Bearded Iris (Historic 1936 Dykes Medal Salmon-Pink Blend Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Mary Geddes Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Mary Geddes was bred by Mrs. Edward C. Stahlman with T.A. Washington and introduced in 1931, blending light ochraceous-salmon standards with falls stained a deeper reddish tone for an overall brilliant orange-salmon garden effect. It carries purple-based foliage, reliable four-way branching, and long-lasting bloom that made it a favorite for cut arrangements. It received the AIS and RHS Wisley Awards of Merit in 1933 and the American Dykes Medal in 1936. Divide every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Cherie Bearded Iris (Historic 1951 Dykes Medal Flamingo-Pink Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Cherie Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Cherie, hybridized by David Hall and registered in 1945, is a large, ruffled, full-bodied flamingo-pink self with a deep tangerine beard and excellent form and substance. Vigorous with much-above-average increase and stout, well-branched stems, it won the Award of Merit in 1949 and the American Dykes Medal in 1951, and became an important breeding parent behind many later pink cultivars. Divide every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Sable Night Bearded Iris (Historic 1955 Dykes Medal Black-Purple Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Sable Night Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Sable Night, hybridized by Paul Cook and registered in 1950, bears very deep maroon-purple standards over solid black falls tinted maroon-purple, with a dark brown beard, on large five-inch, glossy-textured blooms. Hailed on introduction as one of the most sensational black irises yet raised, it took the Award of Merit in 1954 and the American Dykes Medal in 1955. Divide every three to four years after bloom to keep clumps vigorous.

common_name: Mary Randall Bearded Iris (Historic 1954 Dykes Medal Rose-Pink Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Mary Randall Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Mary Randall, hybridized by Orville Fay from 'New Horizon' crossed with an F2 pink seedling ('Pink Cameo' x 'Cherie') and registered in 1950, is a deep rose-pink self with a bright red-tangerine beard and remarkably thick, wide, flaring falls free of markings. It won the Award of Merit in 1953 and the American Dykes Medal in 1954, and remained among the most sought-after flamingo pinks for its outstanding seedling-producing ability. Divide every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Allegiance Bearded Iris (Historic 1964 Dykes Medal Dark Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Allegiance Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Allegiance, hybridized by Paul Cook from 'Dark Boatman' crossed with a seedling descended from 'Distance' and 'Pierre Menard', and registered in 1957, carries violet-ultramarine standards over Roslyn-blue falls with a medium blue, yellow-tipped beard. Long regarded as the standard of comparison for ultra-dark blue bearded iris, it won the Award of Merit in 1960 and the American Dykes Medal in 1964. Divide every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Winter Olympics Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Reblooming White Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Winter Olympics Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Winter Olympics, hybridized by Opal Brown from 'Poet's Dream' crossed with 'Eleanor's Pride' and registered in 1961, is a pure white self with a white beard and excellent early-to-midseason bloom. It has documented rebloom capability as far south as USDA Zone 8a and became an influential parent used on both sides of many later white and pastel crosses. It earned the Award of Merit in 1966 and the American Dykes Medal in 1967. Divide every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Song of Norway Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Silvery Powder-Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Song of Norway Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Song of Norway, hybridized by Walter Luihn from 'Nobleman' crossed with 'Blue Luster' and registered in 1977, opens a ruffled silvery light powder-blue self that lightens further as the bloom matures, with a deep bluebird-blue, silver-tipped beard that stands out against the pale petals. Exceptional branching can hold up to five open flowers at once, a trait especially prized on the show bench. It received the Award of Merit in 1983 and the American Dykes Medal in 1986. Divide every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Brown Lasso Border Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Butterscotch-and-Violet Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Brown Lasso Border Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Brown Lasso, hybridized by Eugene Buckles with David Niswonger from 'Punchline' crossed with a seedling of 'Wild Mustang' and 'Milestone', and registered in 1972, is a compact 22-inch Border Bearded iris with deep butterscotch standards and light violet falls sharply edged in medium brown around a yellow beard, an unusual color combination for its class. It swept AIS honors through the late 1970s and became the first Border Bearded cultivar to win the American Dykes Medal, in 1981, ahead of many taller Tall Bearded rivals. Its shorter stature suits smaller borders and front-of-bed plantings. Divide every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Mystique Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Blue Bitone Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Mystique Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Mystique, hybridized by Joseph Ghio from a complex multi-generation blue breeding line and registered in 1972, bears light blue standards with a deep blue-purple midrib over deep blue-purple falls and a matching blue beard. It swept AIS Judges' Choice honors in 1976 and 1977, earned the Award of Merit in 1978, and won the American Dykes Medal in 1980. Divide every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor.

common_name: Celebration Song Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Reblooming Apricot-and-Lavender Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Celebration Song Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Celebration Song, from Schreiner's Gardens, is a bitone from 'Lullaby Of Spring' crossed with 'Frances Gaulter' and was introduced in 1993, with apricot-pink standards over blue-lavender falls paling toward the center to set off a tangerine beard. Remarkably vigorous, it produces three to four stems and nine to twelve buds per plant and reblooms reliably across a wide range of climates. It won the Wister Medal in 2000 and the American Dykes Medal in 2003. Divide every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Crowned Heads Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Reverse Neglecta Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Crowned Heads Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Crowned Heads, hybridized by Keith Keppel from 'In Reverse' crossed with 'Honky Tonk Blues' and registered in 1996, shows a reverse neglecta pattern of wisteria-violet standards over falls that open light blue, shade deeper in the heart, and age to a silvery blue-white, with a blue beard and goldenrod throat and a slight sweet fragrance. It won the Wister Medal in 2003 and the American Dykes Medal in 2004. Divide every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Queen's Circle Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning White Iris with Blue-Edged Falls)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Queen's Circle Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Queen's Circle, hybridized by Fred Kerr from 'Victoria Circle' crossed with 'Christiana Baker' and registered in 1999, bears crisp white standards and white falls edged in dark blue, with an orange-red beard fading to pale yellow at the tip. It reblooms in Zone 9-10 California gardens, ranked #2 in the 2010 AIS Tall Bearded Symposium popularity poll, and won the Wister Medal in 2006 and the American Dykes Medal in 2007. Divide every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Florentine Silk Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Peach-and-Violet Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Florentine Silk Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Florentine Silk, hybridized by Keith Keppel from a seedling cross involving a 'Crystal Gazer' sibling and 'Poem Of Ecstasy', and registered in 2004, carries peach standards with a slight orchid basal infusion over medium violet falls edged in narrow pinkish-buff, with a tricolor beard that is light blue at the tip, lavender-white at the base, and carrot-red in the throat. It won the Wister Medal in 2011 and the American Dykes Medal in 2012. Divide every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Dream Lover Bearded Iris (Historic 1977 Dykes Medal Blue-and-White Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Dream Lover Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Dream Lover, hybridized by Esther Tams from 'Miss Indiana' crossed with ('Melodrama' x 'Rippling Waters'), bears clean blue-white standards over dark blue-purple falls with a pale-yellow-tipped blue beard, carried on heavy, well-branched stalks with three buds per socket. Registered in 1970 and introduced in 1971, it won the Award of Merit in 1974 and the American Dykes Medal in 1977. Divide every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Debby Rairdon Bearded Iris (Historic 1971 Dykes Medal Yellow-and-White Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Debby Rairdon Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Debby Rairdon, hybridized by Mrs. Hilbert (Lois) Kuntz and registered in 1964, bears subdued yellow standards with white on the reverse over pearly white falls, praised on introduction for having perhaps the most perfect form in irisdom, with heavy substance that resists wind damage. It won the Award of Merit in 1968 and the American Dykes Medal in 1971. Divide every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Skywatch Bearded Iris (Historic 1970 Dykes Medal Lavender-Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Skywatch Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Skywatch, hybridized by Cliff Benson through a cross culminating in 'Van Cliburn' and registered in 1963, is an immense, extremely smooth, deeply ruffled lavender-blue self with domed standards and broad, semi-flared falls of notably thick substance. It won the Award of Merit in 1967 and the American Dykes Medal in 1970. Divide every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Rippling Waters Bearded Iris (Historic 1966 Dykes Medal Orchid-Pink Blend Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Rippling Waters Bearded Iris is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Rippling Waters, hybridized by Orville Fay and registered in 1961, blends blue-orchid and pink tones into a soft self capped with a bold tangerine-red beard, with piecrust ruffling encircling every bloom. It swept the Judges' Choice First Place award in both 1962 and 1963, took the Award of Merit in 1964, and won the American Dykes Medal in 1966. Divide every three to four years after bloom.
